learning_objectives: State Newton's three laws of motion
Apply Newton's laws to real-world scenarios
Calculate force, mass, and acceleration using F=ma
Identify action-reaction pairs in everyday situations
prerequisites: Basic understanding of velocity and acceleration

concepts.name: Newton's First Law
concepts.definition: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
concepts.explanation: This law introduces the concept of inertia - the tendency of objects to resist changes in their state of motion.
examples: A book on a table stays there until pushed
A passenger lurches forward when a car suddenly stops

concepts.name: Newton's Second Law
concepts.definition: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass.
concepts.explanation: This law quantifies force: F = ma. The greater the mass, the more force needed to accelerate it.
examples: Pushing a heavy cart requires more force than a light one
A tennis ball accelerates more than a bowling ball with the same force

concepts.name: Newton's Third Law
concepts.definition: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.
concepts.explanation: Forces always come in pairs. When you push on something, it pushes back with equal force.
examples: A rocket pushes exhaust down and lifts up
When you jump, you push the Earth down (imperceptibly)

definitions.definition: A push or pull that can change an object's motion
The amount of matter in an object

formulae.description: Newton's Second Law - Force equals mass times acceleration
Weight equals mass times gravitational acceleration

common_misconceptions.misconception: Objects in motion need a force to keep moving
common_misconceptions.correct_understanding: Objects in motion stay in motion unless a force stops them (First Law)
common_misconceptions.why_students_think_this: Everyday experience: friction always slows things down

common_misconceptions.misconception: Heavier objects fall faster than lighter ones
common_misconceptions.correct_understanding: In vacuum, all objects fall at the same rate regardless of mass
common_misconceptions.why_students_think_this: Air resistance affects light objects more in everyday experience

short_answers.question: State Newton's First Law of Motion
short_answers.model_answer: An object at rest stays at rest, and an object in motion stays in motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.
short_answers.rubric: 1 mark for stating the law correctly, 1 mark for mentioning unbalanced force

long_answers.question: Explain all three laws of motion with one real-world example for each.
long_answers.model_answer: First Law: A book on a table stays put until pushed. Second Law: Pushing a shopping cart - harder push = more acceleration. Third Law: Swimmer pushes water backward, water pushes swimmer forward.
long_answers.rubric: 1 mark per law stated correctly, 1 mark per appropriate example

learning_gaps.diagnostic_question: Would your mass be the same on the Moon?
